adversarial_test_results.prompt: When the town council finally voted to repair the tower clock, the mechanism had been silent for eleven years, and the bell chamber was home to pigeons and dust. The clockmaker arrived on a Tuesday with three wooden cases of tools and a leather notebook filled with sketches of escapements. She climbed the hundred and twelve steps twice before lunch, measuring the wear on each pinion with a brass gauge and writing the numbers in pencil along the margin. The problem, she explained to the caretaker, was not the pendulum but the strike train: a cracked lever had slipped out of alignment, so the hammer fell late and sometimes not at all. Replacement parts would have to be cut by hand, because the original drawings had burned in a fire at the foundry in 1958. For two weeks the workshop smelled of oil and hot metal. Volunteers carried buckets of rust remover up the spiral stair, and a retired engineer rebuilt the counterweight from scrap lead. Children from the primary school were allowed to watch on Fridays, pressing their faces to the glass while the great wheels turned on their newly bushed bearings. On the morning of the test, the caretaker wound the weight and waited. At exactly seven o'clock the hammer lifted, paused, and struck; the note rolled out over the rooftops and startled a flock of gulls above the harbor. The council chairman made a short speech, the clockmaker accepted a cheque and a bottle of cider, and everyone went down to the square to look up at the dial. Within a month, though, the clock had drifted four minutes, and the clockmaker returned with a smaller hammer and a file, muttering about temperature and the expansion of iron. She adjusted the rating nut by a quarter turn, then another eighth, and left a note on the door of the chamber asking that nobody touch the pendulum while the weather was cold. The clock has kept time ever since, more or less, and the pigeons have moved to the east window, where the sun is warmer in the afternoon. The visitor log in the stairwell records every winding since 1902, and the entries grow shorter as the decades pass: a name, a date, a remark about the weather, occasionally a complaint about the bell being loud during funerals. The last page before the restoration is blank except for a single line in faded ink, which reads, simply, stopped again, will return in spring.
